newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: Singapore insurance rules may follow industry code.
newsitem.headline: Singapore insurance rules may follow industry code.

text.p: New regulations for insurance brokers in Singapore are likely to follow voluntary standards already put in place by the Singapore Insurance Brokers Association (SIBA), SIBA president Anthony Lim said on Thursday.
"We expect the Monetary Authority of Singapore (MAS) to follow our requirements as a guideline for their regulatory framework," Lim told Reuters in an interview.

The regulations, expected to be put in place by 1998, will bring insurance and reinsurance broking in Singapore under the jurisdiction of the MAS, the country's Minister of Finance, Richard Hu, said in October.
Insurance brokers are currently unregulated in Singapore.
The new rules are part of the city-state's drive to enhance its standing as a regional financial services hub.
Lim said a dialogue with MAS officials had created a framework based on SIBA's own minimum professional standards.

These included a minimum paid-up capital of Singapore $300,000 (US$213,000), minimum professional indemnity insurance of S$500,000, a minimum solvency margin of 50 percent of paid-up capital and separate bank accounts for client premiums.
Lim said SIBA had been successful in establishing with MAS officials that minimum paid-up capital levels would not be increased.
"The majority of brokers already meet these standards and there will be no problem for our members," said Lim.
Another measure MAS could demand is a minimum level of professional qualification for chief executives of insurance broking firms, he said.
Lim said enshrining the principle of professional education in official regulations was "a signal to customers that we are serious about professional standards".

Under the proposed regulations, full details of which have yet to be revealed, MAS has confirmed separate licenses would be required for companies undertaking insurance and reinsurance broking, Lim said.
Consequently, companies must meet the financial demands of the regulations twice.
Lim said he was hopeful that MAS would not require separate companies to be created to service the different sectors.
He also said SIBA had been involved in a dialogue on staggering or reducing minimum capital requirements for brokers requesting both licenses.
"The MAS has been very good at listening to our feedback," he said, adding that some issues remained to be resolved.
